claim: All-equal scores give First Fit, which opens bins too eagerly and wastes the tighter resource. Scoring by the total remaining room AFTER placement makes the job prefer the fullest bin it still fits in (Best Fit), raising utilisation on every family.
change: Replace the constant score with score = -((bins - item).sum(axis=1)): the summed leftover [cpu,mem] after placing the job, negated so the smallest leftover wins.
prediction: Clear score gain; largest improvements on uniform, correlated, small and large where packing density is bounded by total volume.

claim: First Fit ignores the shape of the residual, which is fatal when jobs are one-sided (CPU-heavy vs memory-heavy). Preferring bins whose already-used profile matches the arriving job keeps complementary jobs together and avoids stranding the scarce resource.
change: Score = dot product of the item with the bin's used vector: (item * (capacity - bins)).sum(axis=1). A brand-new bin scores 0, so it is only chosen when nothing fits.
prediction: Big gain on anticorr (one-sided jobs) and bimodal; neutral-to-positive elsewhere.

claim: Minimising total leftover can leave one resource nearly exhausted while the other is wasted, i.e. unbalanced fragments. Minimising the L-infinity leftover keeps both resources equally tight.
change: Score = -np.maximum((bins - item)[:,0], (bins - item)[:,1]) (use capacity-relative residuals if untuned): choose the bin whose worst residual dimension is smallest.
prediction: Gain on large and anticorr (fragmentation of the scarcer dimension is the bottleneck there).

claim: Opening a new bin is free under First Fit, so bins are opened even when a slightly tighter existing bin would do. Penalising the empty (last) row turns equal scores into a fit-aware rule that also discourages needless new bins.
change: Score = -((bins - item).sum(axis=1)) with a penalty added on the always-empty last row: subtract a moderate constant (scaled to capacity, e.g. 0.1*capacity.sum()) from the last row so a new bin only wins when every old bin's residual is worse.
prediction: Gain on uniform and small (many tiny jobs, lots of tie situations); should not hurt any family.

claim: Under the pure max norm the empty last row can tie a fitting bin whose residual equals capacity in one dimension, so new bins are opened needlessly; an explicit penalty on the last row fixes this.
change: Keep score = -max(n_c,n_m) but subtract a moderate constant p (e.g. 0.05) from the last row only, before returning.
prediction: uniform and small excess drop; fewer bins opened early.

claim: Pure L-infinity fit ignores total leftover, so a bin tight in one dimension but wasteful in the other wins ties; adding an L1 term prefers genuinely full bins and cuts waste on large/uniform.
change: score = -(max(n_c,n_m) + w*(n_c+n_m)) where n = (bins-item)/capacity and w is a small moderate weight (~0.25), tuned automatically.
prediction: uniform, large and bimodal excess fall; anticorr roughly flat.

claim: L-infinity controls the worst resource but permits one-sided residuals that strand the other resource, which is exactly what hurts anticorr and bimodal; penalising unbalanced leftovers keeps both resources usable.
change: score = -max(n_c,n_m) - w*abs(n_c-n_m) with moderate w (~0.3), n = (bins-item)/capacity.
prediction: anticorr and bimodal excess fall noticeably; large slightly better.

claim: The hard max is discontinuous in the residuals, so near-ties are decided by one dimension alone; a smooth p-norm blends both dimensions and picks better-balanced bins.
change: Replace max with a smooth p-norm: score = -((n_c**p + n_m**p)**(1/p)) using moderate p (~4), n=(bins-item)/capacity.
prediction: uniform, large and correlated improve via better-balanced choices.

claim: The balance term w*|n_c-n_m| is what made the champion jump (h0007), but a linear imbalance penalty treats a near-tie (0.05 lopsided) and a badly stranded bin (0.4 lopsided) too similarly. A quadratic imbalance penalty strongly punishes bins that would leave one resource nearly exhausted, which is exactly the stranding that inflates excess on anticorr and large.
change: Replace the absolute imbalance with a squared one: return -np.maximum(n_c, n_m) - w*(n_c - n_m)**2, with n_c,n_m = (bins-item)/capacity and w a moderate weight (~0.5), tuned automatically.
prediction: Lower excess on anticorr and large (fewer stranded one-sided bins); roughly flat on uniform/correlated.

claim: The champion minimises the worst residual plus imbalance but never rewards genuinely filling a bin, so on large jobs it can prefer a looser balanced bin over a tighter one. Adding a small total-leftover (L1) term back on top of the balance term (h0005 was flat alone, but the balance term now handles shape) should cut waste on large and uniform.
change: score = -np.maximum(n_c,n_m) - w1*np.abs(n_c-n_m) - w2*(n_c+n_m), with n = (bins-item)/capacity, w2 a small moderate weight (~0.25).
prediction: Lower excess on large and uniform (fuller bins); balance term keeps anticorr from regressing.

claim: The absolute imbalance penalty treats an almost-empty bin and an almost-full bin the same, but stranding matters most when a bin is nearly full and one resource is exhausted. Normalising the imbalance by total leftover (how full the bin is) makes the penalty bite hardest on the near-full lopsided bins that block future placements, targeting anticorr and large.
change: Replace the penalty with a relative imbalance: score = -np.maximum(n_c,n_m) - w*np.abs(n_c-n_m)/(n_c+n_m+eps), with n=(bins-item)/capacity and eps a tiny constant (~1e-6) to guard the division, w moderate (~0.35).
prediction: Lower excess on anticorr and large by keeping the fullest bins balanced and reusable; possible small regression on small if near-full bins are over-penalised.

claim: p0026 keeps bins square but ignores whether the arriving item's shape is consistent with the bin's residual direction. A shape-match bonus (transplanted from p0021, a strong dot-product program) rewards bins whose leftover points the same way as the item, which should drain both resources at the same rate and help one-sided families (anticorr, bimodal).
change: Add a cosine-similarity alignment term to the champion: score = -max(n_c,n_m) - w1*abs(n_c-n_m) + w2*align, where align = (rcn*icn + rmn*imn), rcn/rmn are the residual direction and icn/imn the item direction (both normalised, zero norms guarded to 1). Use moderate w2 (~0.5).
prediction: Lower excess on anticorr and bimodal where item shapes are extreme; may be roughly flat on correlated.

claim: The champion never explicitly penalises opening a new bin beyond the max-norm comparison; h0004/h0006 showed an explicit last-row penalty is at best no-effect under pure max-norm, but with the quadratic imbalance term the empty bin (which has n_c=n_m=1, perfectly balanced) may be over-attractive relative to a slightly lopsided but much fuller bin, hurting large and uniform.
change: Subtract a moderate constant p (~0.05) from the last row only, after computing the full score, so a new bin must beat the best old bin by p to be opened.
prediction: Lower excess on large and uniform (fewer needless new bins), flat elsewhere; small net gain.

claim: The quadratic imbalance term penalises lopsided residuals symmetrically, but a bin that is lopsided toward the resource the arriving item is *heavy* in is more dangerous than the reverse; weighting the imbalance by the item's resource split should target the stranding that inflates anticorr and large.
change: Replace (n_c - n_m)**2 with a weighted version: w_c*(n_c - n_m)**2 where the weight depends on which resource is tighter for the item, e.g. use (max(f_c,f_m)) as a scalar multiplier on the imbalance term, f = item/capacity, keeping the max-norm base and a moderate overall weight (~0.5).
prediction: Lower excess on anticorr and large, roughly flat on uniform/small; net score should improve.

claim: h0010 (shape-match cosine bonus) was flat alone on p0026, but the champion now has a much stronger imbalance term; the alignment bonus should now act as a tie-breaker on the bins the imbalance term leaves close together, which is where anticorr and bimodal lose most.
change: Add a cosine-alignment term to the champion: align = (residual[:,0]*item[0] + residual[:,1]*item[1]) / (r_norm*i_norm) with both norms guarded to 1, and score = -max(n_c,n_m) - w1*(n_c-n_m)**2 + w2*align, w2 moderate (~0.5), tuned automatically.
prediction: Small gain on anticorr and bimodal, flat to slightly worse on small; net score should improve modestly.

claim: The champion's quadratic imbalance penalty (h0009) fixed anticorr but the residual it penalises is measured after placement, so it cannot distinguish a bin that is tight in the binding resource from one that is merely balanced. A term that rewards the residual being close to the item's own shape in the *binding* dimension should sharpen the choice on large and anticorr, where stranding dominates.
change: Add a squared-difference term between the two residual fractions and the item's own resource split: let f_c = item[0]/capacity[0], f_m = item[1]/capacity[1], and add -w*((n_c - f_c) - (n_m - f_m))**2 alongside the existing quadratic imbalance term, with moderate w (~0.4), tuned automatically.
prediction: Lower excess on large and anticorr (fewer stranded near-full bins), roughly flat elsewhere; overall score should improve by ~0.1-0.3.

claim: The shape term only compares the residual's imbalance to the item's, ignoring magnitude, so a bin leaving a residual unlike the item in size is equally scored; rewarding residuals close to the item in both resources packs similar jobs together and cuts slivers on large/bimodal.
change: Add -w*((n_c-f_c)**2+(n_m-f_m)**2) alongside the existing terms, capturing residual-vs-item magnitude and not just difference of differences; moderate w (~0.3), tuned.
prediction: Large and bimodal excess fall; small may improve from tighter grouping.

claim: The empty last row carries no item-scaled cost, so large jobs open new bins too cheaply and leave big slivers; scaling the last-row penalty by the item's dominant fraction makes big jobs fill before opening.
change: After computing the full champion score, subtract w*np.max(f) from the last row only, with f=item/capacity and moderate w (~0.3); tune w.
prediction: Large and bimodal excess fall; new-bin opening on large jobs drops.

claim: A bin whose smaller residual fraction is near zero is effectively dead but is only mildly penalised by the quadratic imbalance; an exponential penalty should sharply avoid creating such near-dead bins, which is where anticorr/large strand.
change: Add -w*np.exp(-k*np.minimum(n_c,n_m)) to the champion score, with moderate w (~0.3) and k (~8) guarding nothing (exp is safe); tune both.
prediction: Anticorr and large excess fall; fewer unusable slivers.

claim: The squared imbalance punishes any residual lopsidedness, even when the arriving item is itself lopsided and such leftovers are correct; punishing only imbalance beyond the item's own split keeps useful bins without stranding.
change: Replace the -0.5685*(n_c-n_m)**2 term with a one-sided form: -w*np.maximum(0.0, np.abs(n_c-n_m)-np.abs(f_c-f_m))**2, moderate w (~0.6); tune w.
prediction: Anticorr and large improve; uniform/correlated stay roughly level.

claim: The base is piecewise linear in the max residual, so it cannot tell a bin that will close from one leaving a moderate sliver. Convexifying the base keeps best-fit monotone but sharpens the trade-off.
change: Replace base = -np.maximum(n_c, n_m) with -np.maximum(n_c, n_m) - 0.35 * np.maximum(n_c, n_m)**2, leaving imbalance, shape and align unchanged.
prediction: Lower excess on large (12.6) and bimodal (7.0).

claim: p0066 beats the champion on uniform (3.98) and bimodal (6.52) but lacks any alignment term; transplanting the champion's dot-product alignment should fix its anticorr without losing its edge.
change: In p0066 add align = 0.3 * (n_c * f_c + n_m * f_m) with n = (bins - item)/capacity, f = item/capacity, keeping its imbalance 0.5685 and shape 0.179 terms.
prediction: Improves anticorr (14.8) and large; may beat -7.511 overall.

claim: The champion's align term rewards residuals pointing along the item, but never rewards complementary fill: a CPU-heavy job should prefer a bin already memory-loaded. Anticorr and bimodal are where this pairing pays.
change: Add comp = 0.3 * (u_c * f_m + u_m * f_c) where u = (capacity - bins)/capacity and f = item/capacity, on top of the existing four terms.
prediction: Cuts anticorr (15.3) and bimodal (7.0) excess; uniform roughly flat.

claim: Constant last-row penalties were flat (h0015, h0017) because opening a bin is cheap when other bins are full and expensive when they still have room. A state-dependent open rule has not been tried.
change: Detect empty rows via np.all(bins == capacity, axis=1); from the full score subtract 0.3 * (1 - mean used fraction of the other rows) on those rows only.
prediction: Fewer needless opens on uniform and small, fewer stranded slivers on large.

claim: h0024 showed p0066 gains +0.083 from the champion's dot-product alignment, best on large. p0067 is stronger on bimodal/uniform and also lacks alignment, so the transplant should pay there too.
change: In p0067 add align = 0.3*(n_c*f_c + n_m*f_m) with n=(bins-item)/capacity, f=item/capacity, keeping its imbalance 0.5558 and shape 0.2129 terms.
prediction: bimodal and large excess fall; anticorr improves.

claim: Best-fit never rewards closing a bin exactly. An exponential bonus for a near-zero binding residual makes the packer actively finish bins, which should cut the large and anticorr excess where slivers accumulate.
change: Add +w*np.exp(-8*np.maximum(n_c,n_m)) to the champion score (exp is safe), w moderate (~0.3), tuned.
prediction: large and anticorr excess fall; small roughly flat.

claim: The champion only looks at the worst residual via max; a bin whose BOTH residuals end small is genuinely tighter for future jobs. Rewarding small residual product sharpens the choice on anticorr and bimodal.
change: Add term -w * n_c * n_m to the champion score (n = (bins-item)/capacity), moderate w (~0.4), tuned automatically.
prediction: anticorr and bimodal excess fall; large roughly flat.

claim: Opening a whole bin for a small item is wasteful; the empty row should be expensive for small items and cheap for large ones, since large jobs have no other home. Champion has no size-dependent open rule.
change: On rows where np.all(bins==capacity,axis=1), subtract w*(1-np.maximum(f_c,f_m)) from the score, w moderate (~0.3), tuned.
prediction: small and bimodal excess fall; large and uniform improve slightly.

claim: p0101 has the best uniform (3.98) and bimodal (6.52) but no closing bonus; transplanting p0093's exponential close term should finish bins and cut slivers.
change: Add +w*np.exp(-k*np.maximum(n_c,n_m)) to p0101 with w~0.33, k~9, tuned; keep all other terms.
prediction: bimodal and large excess down

claim: Quadratic imbalance ignores scale; a log-ratio imbalance punishes lopsidedness hardest in nearly-full bins, which is where anticorr and large strand.
change: Replace imb with -w*(log(n_c+1e-3)-log(n_m+1e-3))**2, keeping base, shape, align; w moderate (~0.6), tuned.
prediction: anticorr and large excess down, others neutral

claim: Best-fit is measured in capacity units, not item units; scaling residual by the item shows how many more similar jobs fit, which matters for big jobs.
change: Replace base -np.maximum(n_c,n_m) with -np.maximum(n_c/(f_c+0.02), n_m/(f_m+0.02)); keep imb, shape, align; tune.
prediction: large excess down, uniform roughly flat

claim: Its constant closing bonus over-commits bins for large jobs (large 12.66); gating the bonus by item size stops pushing big jobs into slivers.
change: Multiply close by (1-np.maximum(f_c,f_m)): close = w*np.exp(-k*np.maximum(n_c,n_m))*(1-np.maximum(f_c,f_m)); tune w,k.
prediction: large excess down, bimodal keeps its gain
